newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam to adjust currency, cut rates - report.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam to adjust currency, cut rates - report.

text.p: Vietnam will adjust its currency and cut interest rates in the months ahead to maintain strong economic growth and tackle a growing trade gap, the official Vietnam Investment Review (VIR) said.
"State Bank Governor Cao Si Kiem told bankers last week that interest rates will be cut further and exchange rates will be raised in the coming months," the weekly said on Sunday.

"He said the adjustment to the exchange rate is necessary as Vietnam has been suffering from a large trade deficit this year," it said. It added that the exchange rate would be "raised gradually to save the economy from a shock".
There was no explanation for what the central bank governor meant by "exchange rates will be raised".
However, foreign bankers said it was clear he meant raising the number of dong -- the local currency -- against other currencies, which would amount to a devaluation.
The official rate of the dong against the U.S. dollar is 11,022. It has been around 11,000 per dollar for more than two years.
There has been speculation for several months that the central bank would allow the dong to fall.
"It's just what we would have expected," a Western banker said in reaction to the VIR report. "A slow drift down in the dong."
The trade deficit stood at a record $3.25 billion in the first eight months of this year, a near-sixfold increase from the same period of 1995.

VIR, of which the Ministry of Planning and Investment is a joint publisher, quoted Kiem as saying that the State Bank of Vietnam would buy dollars to create higher demand for the U.S. currency and bolster its own foreign reserves.
Although the ceiling on loan interest rates was lowered last month, Kiem said it should be cut further to keep in line with inflation.
Vietnam's consumer prices have declined every month since May, taking the annual rate of inflation down to 3.2 percent in August compared with 18.4 percent a year earlier.
The interest rate ceiling on short-term loans currently stands at 18 percent a year and the ceiling on medium- and long-term loans is 18.6 percent.
